name: Phewa Lake
label: Phewa Lake
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lakeside Road' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lakeside Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8202581: large area 'Phewa Lake' (5809 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Pokhara's main lake with Himalayan reflections and colourful boats.

text.description:
Phewa Lake is the big, calm sheet of water that gives Pokhara its postcard look. It is the third largest lake in Nepal, sits at about 742 m above sea level and covers roughly 5.7 square kilometres. The Annapurna range is only about 28 km away in a straight line, and the lake is well known for mirroring Machhapuchhre and other peaks on its surface when the water is still. That pairing of water, mountains and boats is why it photographs so well even on a basic phone.

The easiest place to take the shot is the eastern end of Lakeside, near Hotel Barahi Point. From here the shoreline curves away and the Annapurna and Machhapuchhre peaks can be seen across and along the water to the north, with fewer obstructions than further along the promenade. Out on the lake you may spot Tal Barahi, a two-storey temple on an island, which makes a good small focal point in a wide view. The walkway is a pleasant, easy stroll, but it does get crowded, so be patient for a clear gap at the railing or shoreline.

Take a few frames at different zoom levels: one wide scene with the shore in the foreground, then a closer one of boats or the island temple. If the peaks are hidden in cloud, switch to boats, reflections and the shoreline instead. Check the lens is clean before you start, as lakeside air can be damp.
text.geographic_location: On the north-eastern shore of Phewa Lake in Pokhara, at the eastern end of the Lakeside tourist district, close to Hotel Barahi Point. The lake itself stretches away to the west and south.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops serve this area, so the spot is reached on foot within Lakeside. The lake and your main subject lie to the west of that point. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole shoreline and sky, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of lake and mountains. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the island temple or distant peaks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lakeside Road (eastern end of Lakeside, near Hotel Barahi Point). Phewa Lake with the Annapurna and Machhapuchhre mountains rising behind the water, framed by the lakeside shoreline. Your main subject, Phewa Lake, lies to the west, and the Annapurna and Machhapuchhre peaks can be seen across and along the lake to the north, with the lakeside shoreline framing the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether the mountains or the water's reflection is more interesting. Include a stretch of shoreline or a moored boat in the foreground to give depth. If you want a different view, the island temple of Tal Barahi makes a good second subject, framed by boats and prayer flags with mountains behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the mountains to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the peaks do not wash out. Try a Live Photo to catch rippling water, and use panorama only if people are not walking through the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the best chance of still water and clearer mountains, as haze and cloud tend to build later in the day.

text.access_note: Boat trips and visits to the island temple of Tal Barahi are separate from the promenade walk and need a boat, usually arranged in advance.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning usually brings calmer water and clearer mountain views than later in the day.
Cloud or haze can hide the mountains, especially later in the day or in the wet season.
Standing at the eastern end of Lakeside and looking west, the morning sun is behind you and the evening sun is ahead of you.
The island temple of Tal Barahi can be seen from the lakeshore and is small enough to use as a focal point in a wide view.

name: Sarangkot
label: Sarangkot
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sarangkot View Tower' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Famous sunrise viewpoint over the Annapurna and Machapuchare peaks.

text.description: Sarangkot is a hill on the western side of Pokhara, about 1600 m high, and the standard place to watch the sunrise over the Himalaya. On a clear morning the first light touches the Annapurna, Dhaulagiri and Machhapuchhre peaks, with Phewa Lake and the Pokhara valley spread out below. That mix of snow peaks, water and city makes it work well for phone photos. The best vantage point is the Sarangkot View Tower at the top, where the steps in front of the tower give a good open view. The hill is also known for Manaslu views and as one of the best paragliding locations in the world, so you may see paragliders in the sky. It is part of Pokhara (Ward 18) and has been since 2015. Most visitors drive up, though you can hike up from Miruwa on the Pokhara Baglung highway in about 90 minutes. If you want to avoid the tower's entry fee, the free area beside the Panchmukhi Ganesh Temple is also recommended for sunrise or sunset. Kahun Danda is a quieter hill with views of the range, the valley and nearby villages. Whichever you choose, arrive before sunrise: one reviewer reached the tower just before 5:30 AM and said the crowd grew quickly after that. Cloud can hide the mountains, especially in the monsoon months.
text.geographic_location: Sarangkot is a hill on the western side of Pokhara, in Ward 18 of the city, looking across Phewa Lake and the valley towards the Himalaya.
text.directions_text: Most visitors drive up the hill from central Pokhara; the View Tower is at the top. If you prefer to walk, the hike up from Miruwa on the Pokhara Baglung highway takes about 90 minutes. Set off in the dark if you want to be there for sunrise. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole range, the lake and the valley in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view with the tower steps or railings in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out individual peaks such as Machhapuchhre.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look out at sunrise light on the Annapurna, Dhaulagiri and Machhapuchhre peaks, with Phewa Lake and the Pokhara valley below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower third so the mountains and sky fill most of the picture. Keep a little valley or lake at the bottom for depth. If the tower is crowded, the free area beside the Panchmukhi Ganesh Temple is a good alternative for sunrise or sunset over the range.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky, then slide the exposure down a little so the snow keeps its detail. Hold your phone steady with both hands, and take a few frames as the light changes. Try a Live Photo for a moving moment as the first rays arrive.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, arriving before it begins. One reviewer arrived just before 5:30 AM and found the crowd grew quickly after that. Visibility depends on the weather, and monsoon months often bring cloud.

text.access_note: The View Tower is reported to charge an entry fee and the amount is reported differently, so check the fee on arrival.
claims_not_in_sources: Lowering the exposure slider on bright sky helps keep detail in snow peaks.
A Live Photo can capture the changing light at sunrise.

name: Davis Falls
label: Davis Falls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Patale Chhango' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Patale Chhango' (node/713296203): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Waterfall that vanishes into a deep tunnel-like gorge.

text.description:
Davis Falls, known in Nepali as Patale Chhango or Paatal Ko Chango ("Underworld's Waterfall"), is a waterfall that drops into a gorge and then vanishes into the rock. The water runs through a tunnel about 150 m long, roughly 30 m below ground level, and after leaving the tunnel it passes through Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave. The Phewa Lake dam feeds it. The English name comes from a Swiss visitor who died here in 1961, when her father asked for the fall to be named after his daughter.

It photographs well because the white water, the dark rock and the green gorge sit close together, and you can see the moment the stream disappears. The best view of the full drop is from the viewing platforms and railed cliff path at the top of the falls. Start at the beginning of the path, where the water is at its most striking as it plunges and begins to run into the tunnel.

There are also some fun extra subjects in the grounds, including a model of a traditional Nepali house and statues of people in traditional dress. These make easy, friendly photos.

The cliff walkway can get crowded, so wait for a gap rather than shooting over shoulders. If you have time, the cave nearby offers a very different picture: the underground stream seen through a slit of light. Check current opening status before you travel.
text.geographic_location: Davis Falls is in Pokhara, in Kaski District, Nepal. After leaving its tunnel, the water passes through Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave.
text.directions_text: The falls are in Pokhara; head to the falls grounds. Once you are inside, follow the cliff path to the viewing platforms at the top of the falls and start at the beginning of the path. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole drop of water. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the platform is crowded and you want to include the railings and the gorge. Use 2x to 3x telephoto to pick out the white water against the rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (viewing platforms and railed cliff path at the top of the falls, beginning of the path). The full drop of the white water as it plunges into the gorge and starts to disappear into the rock tunnel.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the main stream along one vertical line, with the gorge wall filling the other side. Keep the railing out of the frame, or use it as a foreground line. Wait for a gap in the crowd before you shoot. For a second picture, the Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave viewing platform shows the underground stream where the falls re-emerge, seen through a slit of light.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white water keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement. Wipe the lens first if there is spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The monsoon (June to September) gives the strongest flow. October to November or March to May may give clearer views. Visit early or on a weekday if you want fewer people on the walkway.

text.access_note: The falls are in a grounds area that may be ticketed, and a temporary closure has been reported, so check current opening status locally or on the listing site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Spray near the falls may mist a phone lens, so wiping it helps.
White water can look too bright in phone photos unless you lower the exposure.
Early or weekday visits may be less crowded.

name: Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave
label: Gupteshwor Cave
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Patale Chhango' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Patale Chhango' (node/713296203): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q31154559: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Sacred cave with a Shiva shrine, opposite Davis Falls.

text.description:
Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave sits in Chhorepatan, Pokhara-17, and is a popular stop for visitors. This photo spot is Patale Chhango, the falls across the road from the cave entrance, about 180 m to the north-east of it. Here the white water of Devi's Falls, also known as Davis Falls, tumbles through a mossy rock channel just before it vanishes underground. The same water passes through the cave, so the falls and the cave make a natural pair. The falls are the outdoor alternative to the cave's underground waterfall view.

The pictures work because of contrast: bright, fast water against dark, damp, green rock. Your phone will cope best if you keep the water from turning into a plain white blur, so tap on the rock beside the falls and lower the exposure slider a little. The cave is also known for its animals. Great Himalayan leaf-nosed bats and fruit bats have been recorded inside, and a British scientific expedition in 1976 catalogued the animals living inside.

Photography is banned or restricted at the main Shiva shrine, and several guides say photos are not allowed inside the cave at all. One guide says photos without flash are fine, so the advice conflicts. Shoot outside and in the entrance area unless staff clearly say you may take photos inside. The waterfall viewing area may close during the monsoon because of flooding.
text.geographic_location: In Chhorepatan, Pokhara-17, on the Siddhartha Highway.
text.directions_text: The site is on the Siddhartha Highway in Chhorepatan, Pokhara-17. Ask for Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave or Devi's Falls. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the falls and the mossy channel as a whole. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the rushing water and the rock texture without leaning over any barrier. If you go to the cave entrance, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit the curving orange staircase into one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (across the Siddhartha Highway from the cave, at the falls). The white water of Devi's Falls rushing through a mossy rock channel just before it disappears underground, seen from the road side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the channel along one of the lines so the water leads the eye into the frame. Include some of the green rock on both sides to show the size of the falls. For a different picture, walk about 180 m south-west to the cave entrance and photograph the orange spiral staircase with its carved deity figures, as long as you stay in the areas where photos are allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rock next to the water to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly to keep the white water detailed. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water, and wipe your lens first, as spray and damp air can smear it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No time of day is certain here, so pick a time when the road side is not crowded. Even, overcast light tends to suit white water against dark rock. During the monsoon the viewing area may close, so check before you go.

text.access_note: The falls are on the roadside, but the cave is reached on foot from the Siddhartha Highway, and photography is restricted inside, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Even, overcast light tends to suit white water against dark rock.
Spray and damp air near the falls can smear a phone lens.

name: Tal Barahi Temple
label: Tal Barahi Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lakeside' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lakeside nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W120726795 (Tal Barahi Ma V): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Two-storey pagoda temple on an island in Phewa Lake.

text.description:
Tal Barahi Temple sits on a small island out in the lake at Pokhara, so the classic photo is a view across the water rather than a close-up. From the Lakeside promenade, the temple appears on the water to the east, with the shoreline and boats in the foreground. That gives a layered picture: the near edge of the lake, the open water, then the island with its pagoda-style roofs.

It is the easiest place to reach on foot, but it can be crowded, so be patient and wait for a gap along the promenade. At this distance the island will look small at the default lens (1x), so use that wide view for a scene-setting shot with boats and water, then zoom in for a closer picture of the roofs.

If you want the temple up close, with the mountains and their reflections behind it, you need to be on the island itself. That means a boat, so ask locally about the crossing. For a quieter view, Pame is a lakeside area where you can see fishing activity with the temple island across the water.

Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and take a few frames, as boats drift through the scene and change the composition from one second to the next.
text.geographic_location: Tal Barahi Temple is on an island in the lake off Lakeside, Pokhara. The usual viewing area is the lakeside promenade near Hotel Barahi Point.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed here, so head for Lakeside in Pokhara. From there the temple island is straight across the open water to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of shore, boats and island. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the temple roofs closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lakeside (promenade near Hotel Barahi Point). The temple island across the open water, with the lakeshore and boats in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line, so the island sits across the middle of the frame. Include a boat or a bit of shoreline in the foreground for depth. For a quieter alternative with fishing activity, try the Pame side of the lake, where the temple island is also visible across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the island to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and water keep their colour. When you zoom, tuck your elbows in or brace against something steady to avoid blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a sensible choice, as the promenade is likely to be less busy and the water may be calmer. Check the light on the day, as it changes with the weather.

text.access_note: The lakeside promenade is an open public walkway, but reaching the temple island needs a boat and the temple may have its own rules, so check the official site or ask locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: At about 500 m away the temple will look small at the default lens (1x), so zooming in helps.
Early morning is likely to have calmer water and fewer people on the promenade.
Boats moving across the lake will change the composition from moment to moment.
The temple has pagoda-style roofs.

name: World Peace Pagoda
label: World Peace Pagoda
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q13186128: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: White hilltop stupa with views over the lake and the Annapurna range.

text.description:
The World Peace Pagoda, known locally as Shanti Stupa, is a white Buddhist monument on top of Anadu Hill. It is one of the easiest places in Pokhara to get a wide view with a landmark in the foreground. The domed white pagoda stands against open sky, and the hill gives you the lake, the city and, on a clear day, the Annapurna range around it.

The pagoda was built by Nipponzan-Myōhōji monks with local supporters, and the foundation stone was laid on 12 September 1973. Construction was held up for years, and the inauguration came on 30 October 1999. It is about 115 feet tall and has two tiers that visitors can walk around. Four Buddha statues on the second tier were given by Japan, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Nepal. The hill sits about 1100 metres above sea level.

For photographs, the pagoda is simple and bright, with clean curves and a golden pinnacle on top, so it works well against a blue or sunset sky. Then turn round and take the view back over the lake and city. Walk around the pagoda's tiers to find a clear angle, and wait a moment for people to move out of the frame. Photography is welcome, but the site restricts video, so keep to stills and check the current rules at the entrance.
text.geographic_location: On Anadu Hill in the Kaski district, now part of the city of Pokhara. It looks over Fewa Lake and the city, with the Annapurna range behind.
text.directions_text: There are no train or tram stops nearby, so start from Mahendrapool, the main business area of Pokhara, about 7 km away, and go by taxi or private car (public transport is also available). The partly surfaced road from Chhorepatan to the pagoda takes about 25 minutes by taxi or private car. If you prefer to walk, you can cross Fewa Lake by local boat and climb through villages, which takes about an hour. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole pagoda from where you stand. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the tiers, the sky or the wider hilltop. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the golden pinnacle, the Buddha statues and the lake or mountains in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Main platform in front of the stupa, facing Phewa Lake and the Pokhara Valley). The white dome of the stupa in the foreground, with Phewa Lake and the Pokhara Valley spread below and the Annapurna and Machhapuchhre range in the distance. Stand here for a clear view of the white dome and its pinnacle, then move around the pagoda's tiers and paths for other angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pagoda on one of the vertical lines, with space above it for sky. Keep the phone level so the dome and pinnacle do not lean. Use the ultra-wide only if you can keep the edges clear of strangers, because it stretches objects near the edges. For a different shot, face away from the pagoda and photograph the lake and city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pagoda to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the white stone keeps its detail. Take still photos only, since video is restricted here, and check the current rules at the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are the best times, because the hilltop is known for both. Early morning is often the best time to see the mountains, and the evening gives warmer light on the pagoda.

text.access_note: This is a Buddhist monument and active place of worship with restrictions on video, so check the current rules at the entrance and dress modestly.
claims_not_in_sources: Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in white surfaces.
The ultra-wide lens stretches objects near the edges of the frame.
Early morning is often the clearest time for seeing the mountains.
Evening light is warmer on the pagoda.
Modest dress is appropriate at a Buddhist site.

name: Mahendra Cave
label: Mahendra Cave
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mahendra Gupha' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mahendra Gupha' (node/4508316364): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q16977242: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Large limestone cave north of the city.

text.description:
Mahendra Cave (Mahendra Gupha) is a large limestone cave in Pokhara-16, Batulechaur, close to the Kali khola. It is a rare example in Nepal of a cave with both stalactites and stalagmites. Shepherds found it in the 1950s, and it was once known as 'Adhero Bhawan', meaning Dark Habitat. It took its present name after King Mahendra inaugurated it. A team of British cave scientists surveyed it properly in 1976. There is a statue of Shiva inside, and the cave sits at the foot of a green hill where horses and mules are often seen grazing.

The most useful outdoor photo is at the cave mouth at the top of the stairs. Someone standing in the entrance, with the stone steps dropping into the limestone passage behind them, makes a simple frame that tells the story of the place. The spiral stairs down towards the entrance are also worth a photo of their own. The inside is dark and damp, with artificial lighting along roughly half of the accessible passages, so keep your expectations modest there and take your best pictures at the entrance. Photography may be restricted on the stairs, so look for signs and ask staff. If you have time, the Kumari Cave and the Bat Cave are close by. The Bat Cave is about ten minutes on foot along the trail under the hills.
text.geographic_location: Mahendra Cave is in Pokhara-16, in the Batulechaur area, close to the Kali khola. It lies at the bottom of a green hill, near the Kumari Cave and the Bat Cave.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram-style stops are close by, so go by taxi or public bus. From Pokhara Airport it is about thirty minutes by taxi, and from the Prithvi Bus Park it is about ten minutes shorter. It is also about two hours on foot from the airport. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the person in the cave mouth, as it keeps the entrance looking natural. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the stairs, where space is tight, and keep your phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (cave mouth at the top of the stairs). The cave mouth framed with a person standing in the entrance, with the stone steps leading down into the limestone passage.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Ask your travelling companion to stand in the middle of the opening and turn on the gridlines so you can centre them. Include a few of the stone steps below them to give a sense of depth. Take one version with the default lens (1x) and one with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the space allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your companion's face to focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright outside makes the entrance glare. Inside the cave, try night mode and hold the phone as steady as you can against a wall or rail. If you use a torch, keep it pointing away from your lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in daylight, when the entrance is bright and your companion is easy to see. A softly overcast moment or shade at the mouth makes the contrast easier for a phone to handle.

text.access_note: This is a show cave and visitors may need to buy a ticket or pay a camera fee, and photography may be restricted on the stairs, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Bright daylight at the cave mouth can make a person standing in the entrance look dark, so tapping on them and lowering exposure helps.
Soft overcast or shaded light at the entrance gives a more even exposure on a phone.
A shot taken at the cave entrance in daylight will be easier than one inside the dark passages.

name: International Mountain Museum
label: Mountain Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'International Mountain Museum' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'International Mountain Museum'.
notes: Museum about Himalayan peaks and mountaineering, with a replica summit outside.

text.description:
The International Mountain Museum is Pokhara's museum of mountains and the people who climb and live among them. It opened on 5 February 2004. Inside are three main halls: the Hall of Great Himalayas, the Hall of Fame and the Hall of World Mountains. There is also an exhibition about the Yeti. Outdoors there is a "living museum" about Nepal's indigenous tribes and a 31-foot replica of Mt Manaslu.

For photographs, the outdoor grounds in front of the entrance work best. The museum building sits behind a foreground of statues and the climbing wall replica, and on clear days the mountains rise behind it. That gives you a layered picture with something close, something in the middle and something far away, which suits a phone well. Because the statues and the wall are close to you once you walk up to the entrance grounds, they give the photo a sense of scale and make it look like a place rather than just a building.

A few other spots nearby are also worth a quick photo: the prayer-flag stupa just outside, and the yak statue and monument near the entrance. Take a few frames from the phone icon on the map, then walk toward the entrance grounds to try different angles. If the mountains are hidden in cloud, switch to the statues and the climbing wall and let them be the subject.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Pokhara, Nepal. Guides give slightly different road names for the entrance, so check on the day.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Start from Pokhara town or the lakeside area and go by taxi or hired scooter, asking for the International Mountain Museum by name. Check the exact entrance on the map before you set off. The phone icon on the map is about 190 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the building, the climbing wall replica and the statues into one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a tidier shot of one statue with the building behind it. On clear days, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the mountains in closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 190 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Then walk toward the entrance grounds, near the Manaslu-style climbing wall replica and the statues, for the foreground shots. From there the statues and climbing wall are in the foreground, with the building behind them and the mountains beyond on clear days.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put a statue or part of the climbing wall in the lower corner as a foreground, with the building in the middle and the sky or mountains above. Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line so the mountains get room. If you have time, try the prayer-flag stupa or the yak statue as alternative foregrounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Use portrait mode for a statue close-up, but keep a little distance so its edges stay clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the mountains are most likely to show above the building. If it is cloudy, focus on the statues and the climbing wall.

text.description: Bindhyabasini Temple is one of the oldest and best-known Hindu temples in Pokhara. It is dedicated to the goddess Bindhyabasini, a form of Durga, and sits on top of a small hill. The current building is in the Shikhara style, with a tapering tower. That style is considered older than the pagoda style you see on many other Nepali temples. It photographs well because the whole scene is compact: two golden metal lions beside the gate, a Hanuman statue covered in bright orange-red sindoor powder near the entrance, and the small shrines to Ganesha, Shiva, Saraswati and others around the complex. The temple was established around the 1760s, and the complex also has a lift, installed in 2019, which is mainly used by older and disabled pilgrims. Stone staircases climb the hill from the east, north and southeast. The steps themselves make a good leading line in a photo. Expect worshippers, bells and gongs, so keep your phone low-key, avoid pointing it at people at prayer, and ask before photographing anyone up close.
text.geographic_location: The temple is in Ward No. 2, Miruwa, in Pokhara, Kaski District. It stands on a small hill, with Bindhyabasini park below the temple area.
text.directions_text: From central Pokhara, head to the Bindhyabasini Temple area in Miruwa (Ward No. 2). The stone staircases up the hill come from the east, north and southeast. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate, lions and temple together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower and the sindoor-covered Hanuman statue. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the staircases or a wider view of the complex, and keep the horizon level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Periphery balcony/terrace on the hilltop, city-facing side). The Pokhara valley below with Annapurna and Machhapuchare behind the temple roofline. From here you can see the temple as a whole before you climb to the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the temple tower on a vertical line. Include a few steps at the bottom of the frame to lead the eye up. For close shots, use telephoto on the golden lions or the orange-red Hanuman statue instead of walking up to people. Take the time to wait for a gap in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the temple to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so white walls and gold details keep their texture. Portrait mode suits statues but not people at prayer.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer, with softer light and fewer visitors. Late afternoon can also give warm light on the temple.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress modestly and follow any signs or staff instructions about photography; check the official site or temple committee before you go.
